items.hint1: Think about Genesis 1:26-28. Which created being was given a special place and a special job over the rest of creation?
items.hint2: Sovereignty means supreme rule. Look for the creature through whom God showed his rule by making it in his own image and giving it power over everything else. A thing that was simply made does not show that as clearly.
items.hint3: Eve was made from the man's rib, so she belongs to the creation of mankind rather than coming before it. Between the two remaining choices about people, which one names the whole of humanity that received dominion?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Man

In the CRS syllabus, God's sovereignty in creation is shown most clearly in the making of man. God made man in his own image and told him to multiply, fill the earth, subdue it and rule over every living thing (Genesis 1:26-28). By handing rule to man, God showed that all rule belongs to him first.

How to tell: the word to focus on is sovereignty, not order. Animals and waters were made before man in Genesis 1, so 'first' here means the first clear display of God's rule, which the syllabus links to the creation of man and the dominion given to him.

Why not the others:
A. Eve: she was formed from the man's rib after he was made (Genesis 2:21-22), so she is part of the creation of mankind, not something before it.
C. Rivers: they appear in Genesis 2:10-14 as a description of Eden, not as the act through which God showed his rule.
D. Animals: they were made, but they were placed under man's dominion, so they do not show God handing out rule.

Exam tip: when a CRS question joins creation with sovereignty or dominion, look for the option about man made in God's image and given rule over creation.

items.hint1: Recall the four rivers named in the description of the Garden of Eden in Genesis 2, and where two of them are found.
items.hint2: The Euphrates runs far to the east of the promised land, towards Babylon. Egypt has its own great river, the Nile.
items.hint3: You should be left with the land of Israel and a region whose name means 'between the rivers'. Which one lies between the Tigris and the Euphrates?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Mesopotamia

The Euphrates and the Tigris are two of the four rivers named with the Garden of Eden (Genesis 2:14). Together they water Mesopotamia, whose name means 'the land between the rivers'. This is the region of Babylon and Assyria, in what is now mostly Iraq.

How to tell: the name Mesopotamia itself describes the Tigris and Euphrates, the two rivers it sits between.

Why not the others:
A. Israel: its main river is the Jordan.
C. Egypt: its river is the Nile.
D. Canaan: this is the same land as Israel, watered by the Jordan.

Exam tip: link each land to its river. Nile goes with Egypt, Jordan with Israel and Canaan, and Tigris and Euphrates with Mesopotamia.

items.hint1: Recall the last chapter of 1 Samuel, where Saul and his sons fought their final battle.
items.hint2: Each mountain in the Old Testament is tied to one big event. Sinai goes with the Law, and Zion with Jerusalem, the city of David.
items.hint3: One of the two remaining mountains is where Elijah called down fire from heaven. The other is where Saul fell. Which is which?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Gilboa

Saul's reign ended in defeat. The Philistines fought Israel, killed Saul's sons, and wounded Saul, who then fell on his own sword on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:1-6). His death completed his rejection by God after his disobedience.

How to tell: 1 Samuel 31 names Mount Gilboa as the place where Israel fled before the Philistines and Saul and his sons died.

Why not the others:
A. Sinai: this is where God gave the Law to Moses.
B. Zion: this is the hill of Jerusalem, the city David captured.
D. Carmel: this is where Elijah defeated the prophets of Baal.

Exam tip: learn Old Testament mountains as pairs with one event each: Sinai and the Law, Carmel and Elijah, Gilboa and Saul's death, Zion and Jerusalem.

items.hint1: A religious reform is a change that cleans up worship. Think of what Josiah did after the Book of the Law was read to him (2 Kings 23).
items.hint2: Check each option against Josiah's time. Some belong to stories that happened hundreds of years before him.
items.hint3: You should be left with two options from Josiah's own lifetime. One is something he did to Judah's worship, the other happened to someone else before the reform began. Which is the result of the reform?
items.solution:
Answer: A. The destruction of idols and high places

Josiah's reform was about returning Judah to the worship of God alone. After the Book of the Law was found, he renewed the covenant, burned the idols and Asherah, pulled down the high places and pagan altars, and kept the Passover (2 Kings 23:1-25).

How to tell: a religious reform changes worship. Removing idols and high places is a change in worship, and 2 Kings 23 lists it in detail.

Why not the others:
B. The building of the Tower of Babel: this is in Genesis 11, long before Israel had kings.
C. The birth of Jeremiah: Jeremiah was called to prophesy in Josiah's reign, but his birth was not a result of the reform.
D. The defeat of Goliath: David did this centuries earlier, in Saul's reign.

Exam tip: for any 'reform' question on Asa, Hezekiah or Josiah, look for the option about removing idols and restoring true worship.

items.hint1: Recall 2 Kings 22, when the Temple was being repaired in Josiah's reign. Who found something important there?
items.hint2: In that chapter, Hilkiah handed a book to Shaphan the scribe, and Shaphan read it to the king. So Hilkiah was not a soldier.
items.hint3: Hilkiah served in the Temple. Of the options that give a religious role, which matches what he did in the Temple in 2 Kings 22?
items.solution:
Answer: C. The high priest who found the Book of the Law

While the Temple was being repaired, Hilkiah the high priest found the Book of the Law and gave it to Shaphan the scribe, who read it to Josiah (2 Kings 22:8-10). Hearing it, Josiah tore his clothes and began his reforms.

How to tell: 2 Kings 22:8 names 'Hilkiah the high priest' as the one who said, 'I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord'.

Why not the others:
A. The commander of the army: Hilkiah was a priest, not a soldier.
B. The prophet who rebuked Josiah: the prophet consulted was Huldah, a prophetess, and she praised Josiah's humble heart.
D. The scribe of Amos: Josiah's scribe was Shaphan, and Amos lived long before Josiah.

Exam tip: learn Josiah's reform team by role: Hilkiah the high priest found the book, Shaphan the scribe read it, and Huldah the prophetess explained God's word on it.

items.hint1: Recall how Josiah's life ended in 2 Kings 23:29, when an Egyptian king marched north.
items.hint2: Jericho and Gilgal belong to the time of Joshua, when Israel first entered Canaan. Think of a place better known for a battle in Josiah's day.
items.hint3: Two places are left: the capital of the northern kingdom and a famous battlefield on the main road north from Egypt. Where would a marching Egyptian army meet Josiah?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Megiddo

Josiah went out to meet Pharaoh Neco of Egypt, who was marching to the Euphrates, and Neco killed him at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29). His servants carried his body to Jerusalem, and his death marked the start of Judah's decline.

How to tell: 2 Kings 23:29 and 2 Chronicles 35:22 both name the plain of Megiddo.

Why not the others:
B. Jericho: this is the city whose walls fell to Joshua.
C. Gilgal: this is where Israel camped after crossing the Jordan.
D. Samaria: this was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel.

Exam tip: tie each king's death to its place: Saul at Gilboa, Ahab at Ramoth-gilead, Josiah at Megiddo.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Kings 18, where Elijah told Ahab to gather the false prophets to Mount Carmel. Two groups of prophets are numbered there.
items.hint2: Elijah called for the prophets of Baal and the prophets of Asherah. Each group has its own number, and the question asks about Baal's.
items.hint3: The two numbers in the passage are 400 and 450. Which one belongs to the prophets of Baal?
items.solution:
Answer: D. 450

On Mount Carmel, Elijah stood alone against 450 prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:19, 22). When fire fell from heaven on Elijah's sacrifice, the people seized the prophets of Baal and Elijah killed them at the brook Kishon (1 Kings 18:40).

How to tell: 1 Kings 18:22 says, 'Baal's prophets are four hundred and fifty men'.

Why not the others:
A. 250: this number does not appear in the Carmel story.
B. 300: this is the number of Gideon's army, not Baal's prophets.
C. 400: this is the number of the prophets of Asherah, a different group.

Exam tip: for the Carmel story, keep the two numbers apart: 450 for Baal, 400 for Asherah.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Kings 17, straight after Elijah told Ahab that no rain would fall. Where did God tell him to hide, and who fed him?
items.hint2: The brook where the prophets of Baal were later killed belongs to the Carmel story, not the start of the drought.
items.hint3: The brook you want was east of the Jordan, where ravens brought Elijah bread and meat. Of the brooks left, which is it?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Cherith

After announcing the drought, Elijah was sent by God to hide by the brook Cherith, east of the Jordan. He drank from the brook and ravens brought him bread and meat until the brook dried up (1 Kings 17:3-7). God cared for his prophet in a time of judgement.

How to tell: 1 Kings 17:3 names the brook Cherith as the first place God sent Elijah.

Why not the others:
A. Jordan: the brook Cherith was east of the Jordan, but the Jordan is the river, not the brook.
B. Kidron: this valley runs beside Jerusalem, not in Elijah's story.
D. Kishon: this is where the prophets of Baal were killed after Carmel.

Exam tip: follow Elijah's journey in order: Cherith and the ravens, Zarephath and the widow, Carmel and the fire, then Kishon for the killing of Baal's prophets.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Kings 11, which explains why God was angry with Solomon and said the kingdom would be torn from his son.
items.hint2: God was pleased with some of Solomon's work, such as building the Temple, so that cannot be his unwise decision.
items.hint3: Rehoboam's own unwise decision came after Solomon died. Of the two choices left, which one turned Solomon's heart away from God?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Marrying foreign women and worshipping their gods

Solomon loved many foreign women, and in his old age they turned his heart to their gods, such as Ashtoreth and Milcom. God was angry and said the kingdom would be torn from his son, leaving him one tribe (1 Kings 11:1-13).

How to tell: 1 Kings 11:9 says 'the Lord was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the Lord'. The cause given is his foreign wives and their gods.

Why not the others:
A. Building the temple of the Lord: God accepted the Temple and filled it with his glory.
B. Killing Adonijah: Solomon did have Adonijah put to death, but the Bible does not give it as the reason God was angry with him.
D. Not punishing Rehoboam: Rehoboam was his son and successor, and his unwise decision came after Solomon's death.

Exam tip: when a question asks why God was displeased with a king, look for the option about turning to other gods. That is the reason the Books of Kings give again and again.

items.hint1: Think about what Jeremiah said to Judah before and after the fall of Jerusalem. Did his message change?
items.hint2: Jeremiah warned of judgement for idolatry, but he also wrote to the exiles about coming home after seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10). Look for a pair that holds both sides.
items.hint3: Dreams and visions describe how a prophet receives a message, not what the message says. Of the pairs left, which one matches warning and promise?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Hope and punishment

Jeremiah's message had two sides. He warned that Judah would be punished with defeat and exile because of its idolatry and unfaithfulness. He also promised that God would bring the people back and make a new covenant with them (Jeremiah 29:10-14, 31:31-34).

How to tell: match each side of the pair to his book. Punishment is his warning of the Babylonian conquest. Hope is his promise of return and restoration.

Why not the others:
A. Law and order: this describes government, not Jeremiah's message from God.
C. Wealth and prosperity: Jeremiah preached judgement on a sinful nation, not riches.
D. Dreams and visions: these are ways a prophet may receive a message, not the content of Jeremiah's teaching.

Exam tip: for the exile prophets, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, remember the double message: punishment for sin now, hope of restoration later.

items.hint1: Hosea's children were given names that carried a message from God to Israel (Hosea 1). Think about what those messages were.
items.hint2: The names were warnings to an unfaithful Israel, not blessings, so be careful with the options that sound kind.
items.hint3: In Hebrew, 'Lo' means 'not' and 'ruhamah' means 'shown pity'. Put the two parts together and match them to an option.
items.solution:
Answer: A. No mercy

God told Hosea to name his daughter Lo-ruhamah, meaning 'not pitied' or 'no mercy', because God would no longer have pity on the house of Israel (Hosea 1:6). Each child's name was a warning about Israel's unfaithfulness.

How to tell: 'Lo' means 'not' and 'ruhamah' means 'pitied' or 'shown mercy'. Put together, the name means no mercy.

Why not the others:
B. Loved by God: this is close to the opposite, the promise in Hosea 2:23 that God would again have pity on 'Not pitied'.
C. My delight: this meaning does not belong to any of Hosea's children.
D. Chosen one: this is not the meaning of any of Hosea's children's names.

Exam tip: learn Hosea's three children together: Jezreel (God sows, and the place of punishment for Jehu's house), Lo-ruhamah (no mercy) and Lo-ammi (not my people). A 'Lo' name is a negative message.

items.hint1: Recall Amos 7:10-17, where someone at the king's sanctuary objected to Amos's preaching.
items.hint2: Amos preached in the northern kingdom during Jeroboam II's reign. Nathan and Hophni belong to the days of David and Eli, long before him.
items.hint3: Two priests are left. One served Josiah in Jerusalem, the other served at the royal shrine of the northern kingdom where Amos preached. Which one?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel

Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, sent word to King Jeroboam II that Amos was plotting against him. He then told Amos to go back to Judah and stop prophesying at Bethel, the king's sanctuary (Amos 7:10-13). Amos replied that he was no professional prophet but a herdsman whom God had called.

How to tell: Amos preached at Bethel in the northern kingdom, and Amos 7:10 names Amaziah as its priest.

Why not the others:
B. Hilkiah, the high priest: he served under Josiah in Judah, more than a century after Amos.
C. Hophni, the son of Eli: he was a corrupt priest at Shiloh in the time of Samuel.
D. Nathan, the prophet: he rebuked David over Bathsheba, long before Amos.

Exam tip: place each person in time before choosing. Most name questions fall apart once you know which king each person served under.

items.hint1: Note the key words 'over the nations'. Look for an event that affected all peoples of the earth, not one nation.
items.hint2: Manna and the parting of the Jordan were miracles for Israel alone, so they show God's care for one people rather than his rule over the nations.
items.hint3: Choosing Israel shows God's choice of one people. Which remaining event touched every nation at once?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Scattered the builders of Babel

At Babel, people tried to build a city and a tower reaching to heaven to make a name for themselves. God confused their language and scattered them over the face of the earth (Genesis 11:1-9). By deciding where the peoples of the world would live and how they would speak, God showed that he rules over the nations.

How to tell: the stem says 'over the nations'. Babel is the one event among the options that affects all humanity, and the syllabus uses it as the example of God's sovereignty over the nations.

Why not the others:
B. Made Israel a chosen nation: this shows God's choice of one people, not his rule over the nations as a whole.
C. Sent manna from heaven: this was God's provision for Israel in the wilderness.
D. Divided the Jordan River: this was a miracle to bring Israel into Canaan.

Exam tip: read the stem's target carefully. 'Over nature' points to creation or miracles, 'over the nations' points to events such as Babel that touch every people.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Samuel 28. Saul faced a great army and was afraid. What did he try first before going to Endor?
items.hint2: Saul's enemy at this time was the Philistine army, so options about other enemies do not fit.
items.hint3: Saul had asked God for guidance before turning to a medium. What happened when he asked?
items.solution:
Answer: B. God did not answer him through prophets or dreams

When the Philistines gathered against Israel, Saul was afraid and asked the Lord what to do. The Lord did not answer him by dreams, by Urim, or by prophets. So Saul disguised himself and went to a medium at Endor, though he had earlier driven mediums out of the land (1 Samuel 28:3-7).

How to tell: 1 Samuel 28:6 gives the reason directly: 'the Lord did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets'.

Why not the others:
A. He wanted to defeat David: the enemy he feared here was the Philistine army.
C. He wanted to defeat the Amalekites: that was his earlier campaign in 1 Samuel 15.
D. He wished to offer sacrifice: his wrongful sacrifice was at Gilgal in 1 Samuel 13.

Exam tip: for 'why did Saul' questions, match the reason to the chapter. Gilgal is the wrong sacrifice, the Amalekites are the spoil he kept, and Endor is God's silence.

items.hint1: These words come from a farewell speech made after Israel had settled in Canaan. Think of which leader brought them into the land.
items.hint2: The speaker gathered the tribes at Shechem to renew the covenant. Moses and Aaron both died before Israel crossed into Canaan.
items.hint3: Two faithful spies entered the land, but only one of them led the nation. Which one gave the farewell speech?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Joshua

Near the end of his life, Joshua gathered all the tribes at Shechem, reminded them of what God had done, and challenged them to choose between the Lord and other gods. He declared, 'as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord' (Joshua 24:15), and the people renewed the covenant.

How to tell: the setting is the covenant renewal at Shechem in Joshua 24, which was led by Joshua.

Why not the others:
A. Moses: he died on Mount Nebo before Israel entered Canaan.
C. Aaron: he died at Mount Hor during the wilderness journey.
D. Caleb: he was Joshua's faithful fellow spy, but he did not lead the nation or make this speech.

Exam tip: link famous sayings to their speaker and setting. A quotation about choosing and serving the Lord in the promised land points to Joshua at Shechem.

items.hint1: Think about how God spoke to each prophet at his call. One prophet is addressed by the same title again and again.
items.hint2: This prophet was among the exiles in Babylon and was told to eat a scroll at his call (Ezekiel 2-3).
items.hint3: Jeremiah is known for saying he was too young, and Isaiah for his vision in the Temple. Of the prophets left, which one was given the scroll?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Ezekiel

God addresses Ezekiel as 'son of man' over ninety times in his book, starting with his call: 'Son of man, stand upon your feet' (Ezekiel 2:1). The title stresses that Ezekiel was a mere human being speaking for the holy God.

How to tell: the title runs through the whole book of Ezekiel, far more than in any other prophet's book.

Why not the others:
A. Jeremiah: at his call he said he was only a youth, and God is not recorded calling him 'son of man'.
C. Isaiah: he saw the Lord in the Temple and had his lips touched with a burning coal.
D. Amos: he was a herdsman of Tekoa, and this title is not used for him.

Exam tip: learn one mark of each prophet's call: Isaiah the burning coal, Jeremiah too young, Ezekiel 'son of man' and the scroll, Amos the herdsman.

items.hint1: Nebuzaradan served Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Think about what Babylon did to Jerusalem in 2 Kings 25.
items.hint2: Joshua led Israel across the Jordan, and Nehemiah rebuilt the walls under Persian rule long after Babylon fell. Those roles belong to other people.
items.hint3: Of the two roles left, one is a priest's work and one is a soldier's work. Which fits the captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Destroying Jerusalem and taking the people into exile

Nebuzaradan was the captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard. He burned the Temple, the king's house and the houses of Jerusalem, broke down the city walls, and carried the people into exile in Babylon, leaving only some of the poorest to farm the land (2 Kings 25:8-12).

How to tell: 2 Kings 25:8-11 names Nebuzaradan as the officer who carried out the destruction and the deportation.

Why not the others:
B. Leading Israel to cross the Jordan: that was Joshua, centuries earlier.
C. Assisting Nehemiah in rebuilding the walls: that happened long after, under Persian rule.
D. Offering sacrifices in the temple: that was the work of priests, and Nebuzaradan destroyed the Temple.

Exam tip: sort names in the exile story by side. Babylonians such as Nebuchadnezzar and Nebuzaradan destroy, while Jews such as Nehemiah and Ezra rebuild.

items.hint1: Jehoahaz was Josiah's son and reigned only three months. Remember who had just killed his father at Megiddo.
items.hint2: Cyrus is the name of a person, a Persian king, not a place, so it cannot be where someone was taken.
items.hint3: Later kings of Judah went to Babylon, but Jehoahaz was removed by the same foreign king who killed Josiah. Which country did that king rule?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Egypt

After Pharaoh Neco killed Josiah at Megiddo, Josiah's son Jehoahaz became king. Three months later Neco put him in chains, made his brother Eliakim (renamed Jehoiakim) king instead, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died (2 Kings 23:31-34).

How to tell: Egypt was in control of Judah at that moment, since Neco had just defeated Josiah.

Why not the others:
A. Assyria: Assyria took the northern kingdom into exile long before, not Jehoahaz.
C. Cyrus: this is a Persian king who later let the exiles return, not a place.
D. Babylon: this is where Jehoiachin and Zedekiah were taken, later.

Exam tip: for the last kings of Judah, remember the direction: Jehoahaz to Egypt, then Jehoiachin and Zedekiah to Babylon.

items.hint1: Recall Daniel 3:8. The accusers were a group of the king's own wise men and officials in Babylon.
items.hint2: The accusers came from Babylon's own people. Nations that played no part in the Daniel stories can be set aside.
items.hint3: The eunuchs looked after the young men's training and food in Daniel 1, not their accusation. Of the groups left, which one was Babylonian rather than a foreign nation?
items.solution:
Answer: C. The Chaldeans

When Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's golden image, 'certain Chaldeans came forward and maliciously accused the Jews' (Daniel 3:8). The Chaldeans were Babylonians, and in Daniel the name is also used for the king's wise men and astrologers.

How to tell: Daniel 3:8-12 names the Chaldeans as the ones who reported the three Hebrews to the king.

Why not the others:
A. The Assyrians: their empire had fallen before this time and they are not in the story.
B. The Syrians: they were Israel's northern neighbours, not part of the Babylonian court.
D. The eunuchs: their chief oversaw the young men's food and training in Daniel 1, but they did not accuse them.

Exam tip: in the Book of Daniel, the Chaldeans are the Babylonian wise men and accusers. For the lions' den, the accusers are the presidents and satraps.

items.hint1: Place each prophet in time. Jehoiachin was carried to Babylon in 597 BC, shortly before Jerusalem fell.
items.hint2: Elijah and Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom long before Judah's exile, so they could not have seen it.
items.hint3: One of the remaining prophets spoke after the exiles had returned. The other was in Jerusalem during its last years. Which one?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Jeremiah

Jeremiah prophesied in Jerusalem from Josiah's reign until the fall of the city. He saw Nebuchadnezzar carry away Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah or Coniah) with the leaders and craftsmen, and he wrote a letter to those exiles in Babylon (Jeremiah 24:1, 29:1-2).

How to tell: the question is about timing. Jeremiah is the only prophet among the options who was alive and in Jerusalem in 597 BC.

Why not the others:
B. Malachi: he prophesied after the return from exile, when the Temple had been rebuilt.
C. Elijah: he prophesied in Ahab's reign, about 250 years earlier.
D. Hosea: he prophesied in the northern kingdom before it fell to Assyria in 722 BC.

Exam tip: when a question asks which prophet witnessed an event, place each prophet in his century first. Most options can be ruled out by date alone.

items.hint1: Jesus raised three people from the dead in the Gospels. Tie each one to the place where it happened.
items.hint2: Lazarus, the brother of Mary and Martha, was raised at their home village. That is not the widow's son.
items.hint3: The widow's son was being carried out through a town gate in a funeral procession (Luke 7:11-12). Which remaining town was it?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Nain

As Jesus came near the gate of the town of Nain, a dead man, the only son of a widow, was being carried out. Jesus had compassion on her, touched the bier and raised the young man, and gave him back to his mother (Luke 7:11-15).

How to tell: Luke 7:11 names the town as Nain.

Why not the others:
A. Capernaum: this was Jesus' base by the Sea of Galilee, where he healed the centurion's servant and others.
C. Bethany: this is where Jesus raised Lazarus.
D. Jericho: this is where Jesus healed blind Bartimaeus and met Zacchaeus.

Exam tip: learn the three raisings by person and place: the widow's son at Nain, Lazarus at Bethany, and Jairus' daughter in her father's house.

items.hint1: Look closely at the words 'Young man'. Who did Jesus speak to, and what was happening?
items.hint2: 'Arise' is a command to someone lying dead or ill. Casting out a demon used a different command.
items.hint3: Jairus' child was a girl, so Jesus did not call her 'young man'. Of the remaining raisings and healings, which person was a young man?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Raised the widow's son at Nain

At the gate of Nain, Jesus stopped the funeral of a widow's only son, touched the bier and said, 'Young man, I say to you, arise' (Luke 7:14). The dead man sat up and began to speak.

How to tell: the address 'Young man' identifies the widow's son. Each raising and healing has its own words.

Why not the others:
A. Healed Jairus' daughter: Jesus said 'Talitha cumi', meaning 'Little girl, I say to you, arise'.
C. Healed the man at Bethesda: Jesus said 'Rise, take up your pallet, and walk'.
D. Cast out demons in the synagogue: Jesus said 'Be silent, and come out of him'.

Exam tip: in 'who said this' miracle questions, the way the person is addressed (young man, little girl, a name) usually points to the answer.

items.hint1: Recall Luke 24:13-35. Two disciples walked to Emmaus and a stranger joined them. Who was he, and what had just happened?
items.hint2: On that road, the disciples met Jesus alive again and knew him when he broke bread. So the event must come after the one that made this possible.
items.hint3: Jesus was killed and later went up to heaven. The Emmaus walk fits between two events. Which one had happened that very morning?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Jesus' resurrection

On the day Jesus rose from the dead, Cleopas and another disciple were walking to Emmaus. The risen Jesus joined them, explained the Scriptures about himself, and was recognised when he broke bread with them (Luke 24:13-35). The walk is one of the resurrection appearances.

How to tell: Luke 24 places it on the same day the women found the tomb empty. It happened after he rose and before he ascended.

Why not the others:
A. Jesus' birth: this is true in time, but the story is about meeting the risen Jesus, not about his birth.
B. Jesus' crucifixion: it did come after the crucifixion, but a dead Jesus could not walk with them. The event it follows directly is the resurrection.
D. Jesus' ascension: after the ascension Jesus no longer appeared on earth in this way, and Emmaus came before it.

Exam tip: for 'took place after' questions, pick the event immediately before, the one the story depends on, not just any earlier event.

items.hint1: Recall Paul's first missionary journey in Acts 13, when the team reached the island of Cyprus.
items.hint2: At Paphos, a magician tried to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus away from the faith. Two missionaries were preaching there, but only one spoke the judgement.
items.hint3: Peter was not on this journey. Of the two leaders of the journey, which one, filled with the Holy Spirit, told Elymas he would be blind?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Paul

At Paphos in Cyprus, Elymas the magician opposed Paul and Barnabas and tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Saul, also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, called him a son of the devil and declared he would be blind for a time. Mist and darkness fell on Elymas, and the proconsul believed (Acts 13:6-12).

How to tell: Acts 13:9 names 'Saul, who is also called Paul' as the speaker.

Why not the others:
A. Peter: he dealt with Simon the magician in Samaria, not Elymas.
C. Barnabas: he was with Paul at Paphos, but Paul pronounced the blindness.
D. John: John Mark was only their helper on this journey, and the apostle John was not there.

Exam tip: do not mix up the two magicians in Acts: Simon in Samaria faced Peter, and Elymas at Paphos faced Paul.

items.hint1: Recall Acts 12:20-23, the death of Herod. Why were people trying to please him?
items.hint2: The people shouting depended on Herod's land for their food and wanted peace with him. So they came from outside his own territory.
items.hint3: Judea and Jerusalem were Herod's own territory, and he came down from there to Caesarea to give the speech. Of the options left, which people are named in Acts 12:20 as depending on his country for food?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Tyre and Sidon

Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, who depended on his country for food. They came to ask for peace. When Herod made a speech in royal robes, they shouted, 'The voice of a god, and not of man'. Because he did not give God the glory, an angel struck him and he died (Acts 12:20-23).

How to tell: Acts 12:20 names Tyre and Sidon as the people seeking his favour.

Why not the others:
A. Capernaum: this Galilean town is not in the story.
C. Jerusalem: Herod killed James and arrested Peter there, but the speech was at Caesarea.
D. Judea: Herod came down from Judea to Caesarea, but the flatterers were not Judeans.

Exam tip: when a Bible question asks where people came from, separate the place of the event (Caesarea) from the home of the people (Tyre and Sidon).

items.hint1: Recall Acts 19:23-41, the riot at Ephesus. Why would preaching against idols make someone angry?
items.hint2: The opposition at Ephesus came from a tradesman who made silver shrines of the goddess Artemis. He was losing business.
items.hint3: Gamaliel and Agrippa are linked with Jerusalem and Caesarea. Of the two remaining names, which one belongs to the silversmith?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Demetrius

At Ephesus, Paul's preaching that gods made with hands are not gods hurt the trade of those who made silver shrines of Artemis. Demetrius, a silversmith, gathered the craftsmen and stirred up a riot in the theatre (Acts 19:23-29).

How to tell: the opposition was about money and idols, and Acts 19:24 names Demetrius as the silversmith who led it.

Why not the others:
A. Agrippa: he was the king who heard Paul's defence at Caesarea.
B. Gamaliel: he was the Pharisee teacher at Jerusalem who advised the council to leave the apostles alone.
D. Ananias: the men of this name in Acts are the disciple at Damascus, the man who lied with Sapphira and a high priest at Jerusalem, none of them at Ephesus.

Exam tip: link Paul's persecutions to their city: Philippi to the slave girl's owners, Ephesus to Demetrius the silversmith, and Jerusalem to the Jews in the Temple.

items.hint1: Recall Acts 27-28, Paul's journey as a prisoner to Rome, the storm and the shipwreck.
items.hint2: The ship sailed past one of these islands before the storm struck, and another island is where John saw the Revelation. Neither is where the ship was wrecked.
items.hint3: Of the two islands left, one was visited on Paul's first missionary journey and the other only on his voyage as a prisoner. Which fits a shipwreck on the way to Rome?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Malta

On the way to Rome, Paul's ship was caught in a storm and wrecked, but all on board reached land safely. On the island of Malta (called Melita in some Bibles), a viper fastened on Paul's hand as he gathered sticks. He shook it off and suffered no harm, and the islanders said he was a god (Acts 28:1-6).

How to tell: Acts 28:1 says 'the island was called Malta'.

Why not the others:
A. Cyprus: Paul visited it on his first journey, where Elymas was blinded.
C. Crete: the ship sailed along Crete before the storm drove it away.
D. Patmos: this is where John received the Book of Revelation.

Exam tip: for Paul's islands, remember Cyprus on the first journey, Crete before the storm, and Malta after the shipwreck.

items.hint1: The Sadducees were a Jewish group who often disagreed with the Pharisees. Think of what they asked Jesus about a woman married to seven brothers (Mark 12:18-23).
items.hint2: The Sadducees held firmly to the Law of Moses, so they did not deny it. Look for the teaching the Gospels name every time the Sadducees appear.
items.hint3: Acts 23:8 mentions two ideas the Sadducees rejected, but the Gospels name one of them again and again. Which one did their question to Jesus test?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Resurrection

The Sadducees were a priestly Jewish group who accepted the Law of Moses but denied that the dead would rise. The Gospels introduce them as those 'who say there is no resurrection' (Matthew 22:23, Mark 12:18), and in Acts they were annoyed that the apostles preached the resurrection (Acts 4:1-2).

How to tell: the resurrection is the belief linked with the Sadducees every time they appear in the Gospels and Acts, so it is the doctrine the question is looking for.

Why not the others:
A. Angels: Acts 23:8 does say they also denied angels, but this is mentioned once as an addition, and it is not the doctrine they are known for.
B. Prophecy: this is not given in the Bible as a belief the Sadducees denied.
D. The Law of Moses: the Sadducees accepted it and treated it as their main authority.

Exam tip: when two options both have some support, choose the one the Bible stresses most often about that group. For the Sadducees, that is their denial of the resurrection.

items.hint1: Recall 1 Corinthians 12:28, where Paul lists the roles God has appointed in the Church in numbered order: first, second, third.
items.hint2: One of these roles is listed in Ephesians 4:11, not in the Corinthians list, so it cannot hold a numbered place there.
items.hint3: Paul's list begins with apostles and then prophets. What comes next?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Teacher

In 1 Corinthians 12:28, Paul says God has appointed in the Church 'first apostles, second prophets, third teachers', then workers of miracles, healers, helpers, administrators and speakers in tongues. He uses the list to show that the one body has many parts, each with its own role.

How to tell: count along the list: apostles 1st, prophets 2nd, teachers 3rd.

Why not the others:
A. Apostle: this is first in the list.
B. Prophet: this is second in the list.
D. Evangelist: this role appears in Ephesians 4:11, not in the Corinthians list.

Exam tip: when a question asks about order 'according to Paul in Corinthians', use 1 Corinthians 12:28. Evangelists and pastors belong to the Ephesians 4:11 list.

items.hint1: Recall Acts 10, where a Roman centurion had a vision and sent for Peter. Where did the centurion live, and where was Peter staying?
items.hint2: Cornelius lived in a coastal city that was the Roman headquarters in Judea. Cities Paul reached on his later journeys are too far away.
items.hint3: Two places are left. One is a small village near Jerusalem, the other was the Roman government's city on the coast. Where would a Roman army officer be based?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Caesarea

Cornelius was a centurion of the Italian Cohort who feared God, gave alms and prayed. He lived at Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea (Acts 10:1). An angel told him to send to Joppa for Peter, and when Peter preached in his house the Holy Spirit fell on the Gentiles who were listening.

How to tell: Acts 10:1 says, 'At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius'.

Why not the others:
A. Ephesus: this is where Paul preached and Demetrius caused a riot.
B. Corinth: this is where Paul stayed with Aquila and Priscilla.
D. Bethany: this is the village of Mary, Martha and Lazarus.

Exam tip: keep the two places in the Cornelius story apart: Peter was at Joppa, and Cornelius was at Caesarea.

items.hint1: Think of the day Mary and Joseph brought the baby Jesus to the Temple in Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (Luke 2).
items.hint2: Two elderly people met the child at the Temple that day: Simeon, and then Anna. Mary's relative in Luke is Elizabeth, not Anna, and Jairus belongs to a different story, so Anna is described by a title, not by a family link.
items.hint3: Two titles remain. In Israel, priests came from the men of Aaron's family. Which title fits a woman who spoke God's message and told others about the child?
items.solution:
Answer: A. A prophetess

A prophet or prophetess is someone who speaks God's message to people. Luke 2:36-38 calls Anna, daughter of Phanuel of the tribe of Asher, a prophetess. She was an old widow who worshipped in the Temple day and night with fasting and prayer.

How to tell: when the infant Jesus was presented at the Temple, Anna came up, gave thanks to God and spoke about the child to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem. Luke names her with the title 'prophetess' in 2:36.

Why not the others:
B. A priestess: in Israel the priests were men from the family of Aaron, and Luke gives Anna no such role.
C. Mary's cousin from Bethlehem: Mary's relative in Luke 1 is Elizabeth, who lived in the hill country of Judea.
D. The widow of Jairus: Anna was a widow, but Jairus was the synagogue ruler whose daughter Jesus raised, and he appears in a different story.

Exam tip: at the presentation in the Temple, pair the two witnesses: Simeon, the righteous man who took the child in his arms and praised God, and Anna, the prophetess. Watch for options that swap in Elizabeth or other women from nearby stories.

items.hint1: Recall the scene in Acts 5 where the apostles stood before the Jewish council, and a respected Pharisee and teacher of the law stood up to give advice.
items.hint2: Gamaliel pointed to two men, Theudas and Judas the Galilean, who each gathered followers. Ask what happened to their movements in the end, and what lesson he drew from that for the council.
items.hint3: Gamaliel's advice was to leave the apostles alone, not to silence them, and he said nothing in praise of Theudas. Which option matches the lesson that a movement's success depends on where it comes from?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Human plans fail if not from God

Gamaliel argued that a movement started only by people will collapse by itself, but one that comes from God cannot be stopped, and fighting it would be fighting God (Acts 5:38-39).

How to tell: Theudas claimed to be somebody and about four hundred men followed him, but he was killed and his followers scattered. Judas the Galilean also perished and his followers were dispersed. From these two examples Gamaliel told the council, 'Keep away from these men and let them alone.'

Why not the others:
B. Christians should stop preaching: Gamaliel advised the council to let the apostles alone, and the apostles kept preaching.
C. Prophets were always false: Gamaliel made no claim about prophets in general, only about movements that are not from God.
D. Theudas was greater than Moses: Theudas was used as an example of failure, and Moses is not mentioned in the speech.

Exam tip: when a question asks why a speaker cited an example, first recall how the example ended. Here both leaders died and their followers scattered, so the lesson is about human efforts failing.

items.hint1: The picture of putting on humility like clothing comes with a reason drawn from the Old Testament, about how God treats two kinds of people.
items.hint2: The reason is a proverb that both 1 Peter 5:5 and James 4:6 quote. It is about a person's standing before God, not about worldly gain.
items.hint3: Riches and power are worldly rewards, so set them aside. Between a Jewish custom and a statement about how God treats the proud and the humble, which is the reason the verse actually quotes from Proverbs 3:34?
items.solution:
Answer: A. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble

Believers are told to put on humility because God resists people who exalt themselves but gives his favour, called grace, to those who are humble. This quotes Proverbs 3:34.

How to tell: the exact words 'clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble' are in 1 Peter 5:5, and James 4:6 quotes the same proverb. Paul uses the same clothing picture in Colossians 3:12, where believers are to put on humility. The question loosely credits Paul, but the reason it asks for is the one in option A.

Why not the others:
B. Humility brings material riches: the passage promises God's grace and being lifted up in due time, not wealth.
C. It was the tradition of the Jews: the reason given is God's attitude to the proud and the humble, not a custom.
D. It leads to political power: humility is taught as a way to live before God and others, not a route to power.

Exam tip: when the New Testament gives a reason for a Christian virtue, the reason points to God or to Christ's example. Options offering riches, custom or power are usually distractors.

items.hint1: Follow the Emmaus story in Luke 24 in order: the walk on the road, the arrival at the village, the meal, and what happened afterwards.
items.hint2: While they walked, the two disciples did not know who Jesus was, even as he explained what the Scriptures said about the Christ. So their recognition came later, at a particular moment.
items.hint3: Their eyes were opened at the table, and he left only after they knew him. Which action at the meal did the disciples later name as the moment they knew him?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Broke bread with them

In Luke 24:30-31 Jesus sat at table with Cleopas and his companion, took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to them, and their eyes were opened and they recognised him. They later told the eleven that he was known to them in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:35).

How to tell: order the events. On the road he explained the Scriptures, but they still did not know him. At the meal he broke bread and they recognised him. Then he vanished from their sight.

Why not the others:
A. Opened the Scriptures to them: he did this on the road, but they did not recognise him then, though their hearts burned within them.
C. Walked past them: he walked with them all the way to Emmaus, he did not pass them by.
D. Disappeared into the sky: he vanished from their sight only after they knew him, and going up into the sky describes the ascension, a later event.

Exam tip: for resurrection appearance questions, put the events of the story in order. The option that happens before the recognition, or after it, is usually the trap.

items.hint1: James ends his letter (chapter 5) with teaching on prayer for the sick and the power of a righteous person's prayer, and he backs it with one Old Testament example.
items.hint2: The example James chose was a man 'with a nature like ours' whose prayer affected the weather over Israel.
items.hint3: Think of the prophet in 1 Kings 17-18 who announced a drought in King Ahab's time and later prayed on Mount Carmel for rain. Which option names him?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Elijah

James teaches that 'the prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working' (James 5:16). He shows this with Elijah, an ordinary human being like us, whose prayer God answered.

How to tell: James 5:17-18 says Elijah prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it did not rain for three years and six months. Then he prayed again, and the heavens gave rain.

Why not the others:
A. Moses: he is not the example James uses in his teaching on prayer.
B. Isaiah: James does not name him in chapter 5.
D. Abraham: James cites Abraham in chapter 2, as an example of faith shown by works, not of prayer.

Exam tip: match each figure to the letter and teaching where they are used: in James, Abraham and Rahab illustrate faith and works, Job illustrates patience, and Elijah illustrates effective prayer.

items.hint1: The question means: whom did Peter urge to endure unjust suffering? Think of the groups Peter addresses in 1 Peter 2 and 3 about how to behave under others' authority.
items.hint2: Peter's instruction to endure pain while suffering unjustly (1 Peter 2:18-20) is aimed at people serving masters, including harsh ones. 1 Peter does not have a section addressed to children.
items.hint3: That leaves two groups Peter does address. One is told to win over unbelieving husbands by good conduct, the other to bear unfair treatment patiently as Christ did. Which group fits 'endure'?
items.solution:
Answer: C. slaves

In 1 Peter 2:18-20 Peter tells servants, or slaves, to be subject to their masters, not only the kind ones but also the harsh ones. If they suffer unjustly and endure it patiently, this is pleasing to God, because Christ also suffered for them and left an example (2:21).

How to tell: the key word in the question is endure. Peter links endurance of unjust suffering directly to servants, and he grounds it in Christ's own suffering.

Why not the others:
A. wives: Peter tells wives to be subject to their husbands so that unbelieving husbands may be won by their conduct (3:1-6), which is not a call to endure unjust suffering.
B. children: 1 Peter has no instruction addressed to children.
D. children: this option repeats B, a printing error in the paper, and fails for the same reason.

Exam tip: in 1 Peter, link each group to its instruction: servants endure unjust masters, wives win husbands by conduct, husbands honour their wives. Look for the key word in the question, such as endure, and match it to the group.

items.hint1: This is an 'except' question. The teaching meant is the famous list of heroes of faith in Hebrews 11, where each person is introduced with 'by faith'.
items.hint2: Hebrews 11 moves through Old Testament history: from the first family, through the patriarchs and Moses, to the fall of Jericho. Anyone outside that list is your answer.
items.hint3: Three options appear in Hebrews 11: an offerer of a better sacrifice, a man called to go out not knowing where, and a woman who hid the spies. Which name does not fit any of these?
items.solution:
Answer: D. Baruch

Hebrews 11 lists people who trusted God and acted on that trust. The syllabus treats this chapter as part of Paul's teaching on faith, although the letter itself does not name its writer. Baruch, the scribe of the prophet Jeremiah, is not in the list.

How to tell: check each name against Hebrews 11. By faith Abel offered a better sacrifice than Cain (verse 4). By faith Abraham obeyed and went out, not knowing where he was going (verse 8). By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish at Jericho, because she welcomed the spies (verse 31). Baruch appears nowhere in the chapter.

Why not the others:
A. Abraham: he is named in Hebrews 11:8-19 for leaving home and offering Isaac.
B. Abel: he is named in Hebrews 11:4 for his better sacrifice.
C. Rehab: this is a misprint of Rahab, named in Hebrews 11:31 for receiving the spies.

Exam tip: in 'except' questions on a list chapter, tick off the names you can place in the list. The one you cannot place, often a less familiar name from elsewhere in the Bible, is the answer.

items.hint1: Paul often worked with his own hands so that he would not be a burden to the churches. Think of where Acts tells us what his trade was.
items.hint2: At Corinth Paul stayed with Aquila and Priscilla, a couple who had come from Italy, because they shared the same trade (Acts 18:1-3).
items.hint3: Fishing was the trade of Peter, Andrew, James and John. What did Aquila, Priscilla and Paul make?
items.solution:
Answer: B. tentmaking

Acts 18:3 says that Paul stayed and worked with Aquila and Priscilla at Corinth 'because he was of the same trade', and 'by trade they were tentmakers'. Paul used this work to support himself while he preached, as an example of the dignity of labour.

How to tell: the trade is named directly in Acts 18:3, in the story of Paul's arrival at Corinth.

Why not the others:
A. fishing: this was the trade of disciples such as Peter, Andrew, James and John, not Paul.
C. weaving: Acts does not give weaving as Paul's trade.
D. farming: Paul used farming as a picture in his letters, but it was not his trade.

Exam tip: link each New Testament figure to their trade: Peter and Andrew were fishermen, Matthew was a tax collector, Luke a physician, and Paul, Aquila and Priscilla were tentmakers.

items.hint1: Think of the start of Paul's second missionary journey in Acts 15, when he and Barnabas planned to revisit the churches they had founded.
items.hint2: Barnabas wanted to take along a young man who had left them partway through the first journey, at Pamphylia, and Paul refused. The disagreement was so sharp that they parted.
items.hint3: After the split, Paul chose a new companion and Barnabas sailed to Cyprus with the young man. Which option is the one who deserted them on the first journey?
items.solution:
Answer: B. John Mark

In Acts 15:36-40 Barnabas wanted to take John, called Mark, on the second journey, but Paul did not think it wise, because Mark had left them in Pamphylia during the first journey. The quarrel was sharp and they separated.

How to tell: after the quarrel, Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus, while Paul chose Silas and went through Syria and Cilicia (Acts 15:39-41).

Why not the others:
A. Timothy: Paul met him later, at Lystra, and took him along (Acts 16:1-3), so he was not the cause of the quarrel.
C. Silas: he was the companion Paul chose after the split, not the cause of it.
D. Philip: he was the evangelist of Acts 8 and played no part in this quarrel.

Exam tip: for questions on Paul's companions, remember the order: Barnabas and John Mark on the first journey, Silas and then Timothy on the second. The quarrel over Mark is what caused the change.

items.hint1: To find the theme of a short letter, ask what the writer is asking the reader to do. Philemon is a personal letter from Paul about one person.
items.hint2: Onesimus was Philemon's slave who ran away and later became a Christian through Paul. Paul sends him back and asks Philemon to receive him, not as a slave only, but as a beloved brother.
items.hint3: Paul praises Philemon's love and faith near the start, but that is the greeting, not the main request. What two things does Paul want to happen between Philemon and Onesimus?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Forgiveness and reconciliation

The theme of a letter is its main message. In Philemon, Paul pleads with Philemon to forgive his runaway slave Onesimus and to welcome him back as a brother in Christ, so that the broken relationship is restored.

How to tell: Paul says 'receive him as you would receive me' (verse 17), and offers to repay anything Onesimus owes: 'charge that to my account' (verse 18). He asks for mercy and a renewed relationship, which is forgiveness and reconciliation.

Why not the others:
B. Crime and punishment: Paul asks Philemon to show mercy, not to punish Onesimus.
C. Love and faith: Paul praises Philemon's love and faith in verse 5, but this is part of his opening thanks, not the letter's main message.
D. Righteousness and inequity: these are not what Paul writes about in this letter.

Exam tip: for 'theme of a letter' questions, find the writer's main request, not the praise in the opening lines. The request usually names the theme.
